title: How Close Did Your City Come to a Temperature Record Last Month? Tracking ~100 Cities Across North America
text:
Every time this page is rendered (once a month — see the note at the bottom), it:

Takes a fixed list of ~100 cities across the US, Canada, and Mexico (mostly by population, as a standard proxy for “most influential” — see the caveats section for the details and judgment calls involved).
For each city, finds the most complete nearby weather station (the candidate with the longest history and the best coverage of the target month, not just the closest one).
Compares every day of that station’s history against the all-time record for that calendar day — separately for daily highs and daily lows — using an expanding, backward-looking record: a record broken in one year moves the bar for every later year, and never the reverse (see the methodology note and worked example below).
Keeps a running tally since 2020 for both highs and lows, broken out by year.
Focuses on the most recently fully-completed calendar month and, for each city, counts how many days that month landed in each band relative to its record high and its record low — then maps both.
Plots a plain reference map of every city’s location, for anyone who just wants to see where all of them are without any temperature data attached.







Important



This is a live, self-refreshing page, not a one-time snapshot. There’s no server behind it — it’s a static site. At render time, this code re-fetches real station data and recomputes everything below. What you see is only as fresh as the last render (monthly, via cron — see the bottom of the page).

# a single station-year file fails to load -- e.g. a transient SSL/network
# hiccup fetching one year out of a station's multi-decade history -- as a
# WARNING with a full traceback attached. It already handles this
# gracefully on its own (that year's data is just dropped; the rest of the
# fetch continues), so this is expected, recoverable noise, not something
# worth surfacing. Nothing in this notebook configures a logging handler,
# so Python's default "no handler configured" fallback was printing these
# warnings straight to stderr, which Quarto then captures into the
# rendered page. Raising the "meteostat" logger's threshold above WARNING
# silences exactly this, without touching any of *our* own exception
# handling (run_stage/failures) below, which still catches and reports
# anything that actually prevents a city from resolving.

# history, not just the last 30 years -- so this is turned off here on

                         # years behind it before a reading is compared against it at all

TIED_BAND_F = 0.5   # a reading within +/- this many °F of the record counts as "tied" --
                     # NOT the same thing as being within 1°F total spread; +/-0.5°F is a
                     # 1°F-wide band centered on the record, which is what "within a degree"
                     # was meant to mean here. An earlier version of this page used
                     # diff_f >= -1 (i.e. +/-1°F, a 2°F-wide band) for "tied" -- overwritten
                     # to +/-0.5°F once that ambiguity was pointed out.

TALLY_CATEGORIES_MAX = ["Above record", "At record (tied)", "Within 3°F of record"]
TALLY_CATEGORIES_MIN = ["Below record", "At record (tied)", "Within 3°F of record"]


def classify_diff(diff_f, extreme_label):
    """
    Shared classifier for both daily-high and daily-low comparisons.
    diff_f > 0 always means "this day set a new record in the extreme
    direction" -- expanding_daily_comparison() below flips the sign for
    daily lows so this function never has to know which direction it's
    looking at. extreme_label names that direction for the top bucket,
    e.g. "Above" for highs or "Below" for lows.

    The "new record" threshold is diff_f > TIED_BAND_F, not some separate
    number -- it picks up exactly where the "tied" band leaves off, so
    there's no dead zone between "tied" and "record" (an earlier version
    used diff_f > 1 here while TIED_BAND_F was 0.5, leaving diff_f in
    (0.5, 1] classified as neither).
    """
    if diff_f > TIED_BAND_F:
        return f"{extreme_label} record"
    if -TIED_BAND_F <= diff_f <= TIED_BAND_F:
        return "At record (tied)"
    if diff_f >= -3:
        return "Within 3°F of record"
    return None  # not close enough to tally


# Per-city, per-month classification used for the maps below. A 9-step
# diverging ladder -- checked from most extreme (index 0) to least
# (index 8), first match wins. Both ends are fully-saturated anchor colors
# (most extreme in one direction / most extreme in the other), shading
# through progressively lighter tones of the SAME hue toward the middle,
# except for one tier each (index 5) that borrows a light tone from the
# *other* list's hue instead of a plain gray -- see "Why this color ladder"
# in the caveats for why. For daily highs (MONTH_TIERS), red = notable
# heat, blue = far from the hot record. For daily lows (MONTH_TIERS_MIN),
# this is intentionally *inverted* -- blue = notable cold (a new or
# near-record low), red = far from the cold record, i.e. a relatively mild
# month.
MONTH_TIERS = [
    ("#67000d", "3+ days set a new record (>0.5°F over)"),
    ("#de2d26", "1-2 days set a new record (>0.5°F over)"),
    ("#fc9272", "3+ days tied the record (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#fcbba1", "1-2 days tied the record (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#fee0d2", "3+ days within 3°F of record"),
    ("#9ecae1", "1-2 days within 3°F of record"),
    ("#6baed6", "3+ days within 10°F of record"),
    ("#2171b5", "At least 1 day within 10°F of record"),
    ("#08306b", "No days within 10°F of record"),
]

MONTH_TIERS_MIN = [
    ("#08306b", "3+ days set a new record low (>0.5°F under)"),
    ("#2171b5", "1-2 days set a new record low (>0.5°F under)"),
    ("#6baed6", "3+ days tied the record low (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#9ecae1", "1-2 days tied the record low (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#c6dbef", "3+ days within 3°F of record low"),
    ("#fcbba1", "1-2 days within 3°F of record low"),
    ("#fee0d2", "3+ days within 10°F of record low"),
    ("#fc9272", "At least 1 day within 10°F of record low"),
    ("#67000d", "No days within 10°F of record low"),
]


def classify_month(counts, tiers):
    """
    counts: dict with days_above, days_tied, days_within_3, days_within_10.
    Checked narrowest/most-extreme condition first at each threshold, so
    "3+ days" and "1-2 days" versions of the same band never both match --
    e.g. days_tied=5 satisfies both ">=3" and ">=1", but since ">=3" is
    checked first, it's the one that wins.
    """
    if counts["days_above"] >= 3:
        return tiers[0]
    if counts["days_above"] >= 1:
        return tiers[1]
    if counts["days_tied"] >= 3:
        return tiers[2]
    if counts["days_tied"] >= 1:
        return tiers[3]
    if counts["days_within_3"] >= 3:
        return tiers[4]
    if counts["days_within_3"] >= 1:
        return tiers[5]
    if counts["days_within_10"] >= 3:
        return tiers[6]
    if counts["days_within_10"] >= 1:
        return tiers[7]
    return tiers[8]

# Köppen-Geiger climate classification, for the reference map in section 9.
# Data: Beck, H.E., N.E. Zimmermann, T.R. McVicar, N. Vergopolan, A. Berg,
# E.F. Wood (2018): "Present and future Köppen-Geiger climate

# full-globe file at roughly 10x that. Small enough to commit directly
# rather than fetching an external file at render time (this repo's own
# convention is normally the opposite -- see the README -- but a
# few-hundred-KB static classification grid is a different scale of
# problem than the multi-GB weather-model output other posts here
# legitimately fetch fresh each run).

    14: ("Cfa", "#C8FF50"), 15: ("Cfb", "#64FF50"), 16: ("Cfc", "#32C800"),
    17: ("Dsa", "#FF00FF"), 18: ("Dsb", "#C800C8"), 19: ("Dsc", "#963296"), 20: ("Dsd", "#966496"),
    21: ("Dwa", "#AAAFFF"), 22: ("Dwb", "#5A78DC"), 23: ("Dwc", "#4B50B4"), 24: ("Dwd", "#320087"),
    25: ("Dfa", "#00FFFF"), 26: ("Dfb", "#37C8FF"), 27: ("Dfc", "#007D7D"), 28: ("Dfd", "#00465F"),
    29: ("ET", "#B2B2B2"), 30: ("EF", "#666666"),
}
KOPPEN_GROUP_NAMES = {
    "A": "Tropical", "B": "Arid", "C": "Temperate", "D": "Continental (\"Cold\")", "E": "Polar",
}


def load_koppen_layer():
    """
    Returns (rgba_array, raw_class_codes, (left, right, bottom, top)).
    Class 0 (ocean / no classification, e.g. permanent ice sheets) is left
    fully transparent in rgba so the topography layer underneath shows
    through instead of a solid color standing in for "no data." The raw
    codes are returned too so callers (the legend below) don't need to
    re-open the file just to find out which classes are actually present.
    """
    npz = np.load(KOPPEN_DATA_PATH)
    codes = npz["data"]
    left, bottom, right, top = npz["bounds"]
    rgba = np.zeros((*codes.shape, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
    for code, (_, hex_color) in KOPPEN_COLORS.items():
        r, g, b = (int(hex_color[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5))
        rgba[codes == code] = (r, g, b, 255)
    return rgba, codes, (left, right, bottom, top)


def add_topography_underlay(axis, alpha=0.2):
    """
    A muted grayscale backdrop for the climate-zone map: Cartopy's own
    bundled Natural Earth shaded-relief raster (the same image
    ax.stock_img() uses), converted to grayscale and drawn at low opacity
    so it reads as subtle topographic texture rather than competing with
    the climate-zone colors on top of it. stock_img() itself doesn't
    expose grayscale conversion, hence loading the same file directly.
    """
    topo_path = (cartopy.config["repo_data_dir"] / "raster" / "natural_earth"
                 / "50-natural-earth-1-downsampled.png")
    topo_img = plt.imread(topo_path)
    gray = topo_img[..., :3].mean(axis=-1)
    axis.imshow(gray, cmap="gray", origin="upper", transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
                extent=[-180, 180, -90, 90], alpha=alpha, zorder=0)


def in_any_inset(df):
    mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for spec in INSET_SPECS:
        lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = spec["extent"]
        mask |= (df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)
    return mask


def in_main_extent(df):
    """
    A point outside set_extent() doesn't get a marker drawn (scatter
    respects the axes clip box), but annotate() draws its text regardless
    -- so without this filter, a city like Oaxaca that falls just outside
    MAIN_EXTENT (see the caveat where MAIN_EXTENT is defined) would show
    up as a code label floating below the map frame with no dot attached
    to it. Cities excluded here are still fully resolved and tallied
    elsewhere on the page; they just don't get plotted on this map.
    """
    lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = MAIN_EXTENT
    return (df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)


def add_basemap(axis):
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "land", "50m", edgecolor="none", facecolor="#f2f2f2"), zorder=0)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "coastline", "50m", edgecolor="#4d4d4d", facecolor="none"), linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "cultural", "admin_0_boundary_lines_land", "50m", edgecolor="#888888", facecolor="none"),
        linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "cultural", "admin_1_states_provinces_lakes", "50m", edgecolor="#bbbbbb", facecolor="none"),
        linewidth=0.4, zorder=1)


def plot_cities(axis, sub_df, show_labels=True, marker_color=None, s=70):
    """
    Scatter each city's point, optionally labeled with its short code
    (offset in fixed screen-space points, not data coordinates, so labels
    stay a legible fixed size regardless of the axes' zoom level).
    marker_color overrides each row's own "Tier color" with one fixed
    color for every point (used by the reference map in section 9, where
    every dot is plain black rather than tier-colored).
    """
    for _, row in sub_df.iterrows():
        axis.scatter(row["lon"], row["lat"], s=s, color=marker_color or row["Tier color"],
                     edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.5, transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(), zorder=5)
        if show_labels:
            axis.annotate(
                row["Code"], xy=(row["lon"], row["lat"]),
                xycoords=ccrs.PlateCarree()._as_mpl_transform(axis),
                xytext=(4, 3), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.5, zorder=6,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.7),
            )


def draw_insets(fig, df, basemap_fn=add_basemap, marker_color=None, s=70):
    """
    Shared by every map in this post that uses MAIN_EXTENT -- draws the
    Alaska/Hawaii insets defined in INSET_SPECS. basemap_fn lets the plain
    reference map (section 9) reuse this for its own stock_img() terrain
    background instead of the flat add_basemap() the tier-colored maps use,
    without duplicating the inset-layout logic itself.
    """
    for spec in INSET_SPECS:
        lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = spec["extent"]
        sub = df[(df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)]
        inset_ax = fig.add_axes(spec["rect"], projection=spec["projection"])
        inset_ax.set_extent(spec["extent"], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())
        basemap_fn(inset_ax)
        if not sub.empty:
            plot_cities(inset_ax, sub, show_labels=True, marker_color=marker_color, s=s)
        inset_ax.text(0.5, 0.95, spec["name"], transform=inset_ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                       fontsize=7, fontweight="bold", zorder=10,
                       bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.75))
        for spine in inset_ax.spines.values():
            spine.set_visible(True)
            spine.set_edgecolor("#333333")
            spine.set_linewidth(1.0)


def render_temp_map(df, tiers, plot_title, output_path):
    """
    Shared by both the daily-high and daily-low maps below: draws the main
    map plus the Alaska/Hawaii insets, coloring each city's point by its
    assigned tier and labeling it with its short code. The legend is
    drawn on the figure itself as a horizontal band across the bottom
    (`fig.legend(..., loc="lower center")`), not off to the side, so the
    map above it can use almost the entire figure width.
    """
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 9))
    proj = ccrs.LambertConformal(central_longitude=-88, central_latitude=36)
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.005, 0.165, 0.99, 0.805], projection=proj)
    ax.set_extent(MAIN_EXTENT, crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())
    add_basemap(ax)
    plot_cities(ax, df[in_main_extent(df) & ~in_any_inset(df)])
    ax.set_title(plot_title, fontsize=13)

    draw_insets(fig, df)

    legend_handles = [
        plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", linestyle="none", markerfacecolor=color,
                   markeredgecolor="black", markersize=8, label=label)
        for color, label in tiers
    ]
    fig.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0),
               ncol=3, fontsize=8.5, framealpha=0.9)

    fig.savefig(output_path, format="png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)

title: How Close Did Your City Come to a Temperature Record Last Month? Tracking ~100 Cities Across North America
text:
Every time this page is rendered (once a month — see the note at the bottom), it:

Takes a fixed list of ~100 cities across the US, Canada, and Mexico (mostly by population, as a standard proxy for “most influential” — see the caveats section for the details and judgment calls involved).
For each city, finds the most complete nearby weather station (the candidate with the longest history and the best coverage of the target month, not just the closest one).
Compares every day of that station’s history against the all-time record for that calendar day — separately for daily highs and daily lows — using an expanding, backward-looking record: a record broken in one year moves the bar for every later year, and never the reverse (see the methodology note and worked example below).
Keeps a running tally since 2020 for both highs and lows, broken out by year.
Focuses on the most recently fully-completed calendar month and, for each city, counts how many days that month landed in each band relative to its record high and its record low — then maps both.
Plots a plain reference map of every city’s location, for anyone who just wants to see where all of them are without any temperature data attached.







Important



This is a live, self-refreshing page, not a one-time snapshot. There’s no server behind it — it’s a static site. At render time, this code re-fetches real station data and recomputes everything below. What you see is only as fresh as the last render (monthly, via cron — see the bottom of the page).

# a single station-year file fails to load -- e.g. a transient SSL/network

# WARNING with a full traceback attached. It already handles this
# gracefully on its own (that year's data is just dropped; the rest of the
# fetch continues), so this is expected, recoverable noise, not something
# worth surfacing. Nothing in this notebook configures a logging handler,
# so Python's default "no handler configured" fallback was printing these
# warnings straight to stderr, which Quarto then captures into the
# rendered page. Raising the "meteostat" logger's threshold above WARNING
# silences exactly this, without touching any of *our* own exception
# handling (run_stage/failures) below, which still catches and reports

HIST_START = datetime(1885, 1, 1)   # predates nearly every US first-order station's digitized record
STATION_SEARCH_RADIUS_M = 120_000   # 120 km -- wide enough to fall back to a long-running regional
                                     # airport station if the closest site turns out to be short-lived
N_CANDIDATE_STATIONS = 5            # try up to this many nearby candidates per city
MIN_RECORD_YEARS = 20               # a station with less history than this can't give a credible "record" --
                                     # a "record" based on only a handful of years is misleading, not just imprecise
MAX_STALENESS_DAYS = 21             # how far past the target month's end we'll accept a station's
                                     # "most recent" reading -- set generously (3 weeks) since the
                                     # long-running official stations that make the best *record*
                                     # sources also tend to have the slowest final QC/reporting lag
MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE = 0.8            # a candidate station must have data for at least this fraction of
                                     # the target month's days, or it can't support the monthly day-count
                                     # tally below even if its overall history is long
N_WORKERS = 16                      # station fetches are network-bound (calls out to Meteostat's bulk data),
                                     # so fetching them concurrently is a large wall-clock win over serial --
                                     # raised from 10 once the city list doubled to 100, to keep total
                                     # render time from doubling along with it

# The page is about the most recently *fully completed* calendar month, not
# the current (partial) one -- rendering mid-month or later for the prior
# month, per the monthly cron schedule at the bottom of this page, gives
# station data time to finalize before it's used here.
RUN_DATE = datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()
TARGET_MONTH_END = RUN_DATE.replace(day=1) - timedelta(days=1)
TARGET_MONTH_START = TARGET_MONTH_END.replace(day=1)
FETCH_END = datetime.combine(TARGET_MONTH_END, datetime.min.time())

# pandas.Series.loc[] slicing with plain datetime.date bounds is deprecated
# (it now warns and asks for an explicit Timestamp) -- these are the
# Timestamp-cast equivalents used everywhere a date-range slice is needed
# below, so that warning never gets a chance to fire.
TALLY_START_TS = pd.Timestamp(TALLY_START_DATE := datetime(2020, 1, 1).date())
TARGET_MONTH_START_TS = pd.Timestamp(TARGET_MONTH_START)
TARGET_MONTH_END_TS = pd.Timestamp(TARGET_MONTH_END)

MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES = 15   # a calendar day's "record" needs at least this many earlier
                         # years behind it before a reading is compared against it at all

TIED_BAND_F = 0.5   # a reading within +/- this many °F of the record counts as "tied" --
                     # NOT the same thing as being within 1°F total spread; +/-0.5°F is a
                     # 1°F-wide band centered on the record, which is what "within a degree"
                     # was meant to mean here. An earlier version of this page used
                     # diff_f >= -1 (i.e. +/-1°F, a 2°F-wide band) for "tied" -- overwritten
                     # to +/-0.5°F once that ambiguity was pointed out.

TALLY_CATEGORIES_MAX = ["Above record", "At record (tied)", "Within 3°F of record"]
TALLY_CATEGORIES_MIN = ["Below record", "At record (tied)", "Within 3°F of record"]


def classify_diff(diff_f, extreme_label):
    """
    Shared classifier for both daily-high and daily-low comparisons.
    diff_f > 0 always means "this day set a new record in the extreme
    direction" -- expanding_daily_comparison() below flips the sign for
    daily lows so this function never has to know which direction it's
    looking at. extreme_label names that direction for the top bucket,
    e.g. "Above" for highs or "Below" for lows.

    The "new record" threshold is diff_f > TIED_BAND_F, not some separate
    number -- it picks up exactly where the "tied" band leaves off, so
    there's no dead zone between "tied" and "record" (an earlier version
    used diff_f > 1 here while TIED_BAND_F was 0.5, leaving diff_f in
    (0.5, 1] classified as neither).
    """
    if diff_f > TIED_BAND_F:
        return f"{extreme_label} record"
    if -TIED_BAND_F <= diff_f <= TIED_BAND_F:
        return "At record (tied)"
    if diff_f >= -3:
        return "Within 3°F of record"
    return None  # not close enough to tally


# Per-city, per-month classification used for the maps below. A 9-step
# diverging ladder -- checked from most extreme (index 0) to least
# (index 8), first match wins. Both ends are fully-saturated anchor colors
# (most extreme in one direction / most extreme in the other), shading
# through progressively lighter tones of the SAME hue toward the middle,
# except for one tier each (index 5) that borrows a light tone from the
# *other* list's hue instead of a plain gray -- see "Why this color ladder"
# in the caveats for why. For daily highs (MONTH_TIERS), red = notable
# heat, blue = far from the hot record. For daily lows (MONTH_TIERS_MIN),
# this is intentionally *inverted* -- blue = notable cold (a new or
# near-record low), red = far from the cold record, i.e. a relatively mild
# month.
MONTH_TIERS = [
    ("#67000d", "3+ days set a new record (>0.5°F over)"),
    ("#de2d26", "1-2 days set a new record (>0.5°F over)"),
    ("#fc9272", "3+ days tied the record (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#fcbba1", "1-2 days tied the record (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#fee0d2", "3+ days within 3°F of record"),
    ("#9ecae1", "1-2 days within 3°F of record"),
    ("#6baed6", "3+ days within 10°F of record"),
    ("#2171b5", "At least 1 day within 10°F of record"),
    ("#08306b", "No days within 10°F of record"),
]

MONTH_TIERS_MIN = [
    ("#08306b", "3+ days set a new record low (>0.5°F under)"),
    ("#2171b5", "1-2 days set a new record low (>0.5°F under)"),
    ("#6baed6", "3+ days tied the record low (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#9ecae1", "1-2 days tied the record low (±0.5°F)"),
    ("#c6dbef", "3+ days within 3°F of record low"),
    ("#fcbba1", "1-2 days within 3°F of record low"),
    ("#fee0d2", "3+ days within 10°F of record low"),
    ("#fc9272", "At least 1 day within 10°F of record low"),
    ("#67000d", "No days within 10°F of record low"),
]


def classify_month(counts, tiers):
    """
    counts: dict with days_above, days_tied, days_within_3, days_within_10.
    Checked narrowest/most-extreme condition first at each threshold, so
    "3+ days" and "1-2 days" versions of the same band never both match --
    e.g. days_tied=5 satisfies both ">=3" and ">=1", but since ">=3" is
    checked first, it's the one that wins.
    """
    if counts["days_above"] >= 3:
        return tiers[0]
    if counts["days_above"] >= 1:
        return tiers[1]
    if counts["days_tied"] >= 3:
        return tiers[2]
    if counts["days_tied"] >= 1:
        return tiers[3]
    if counts["days_within_3"] >= 3:
        return tiers[4]
    if counts["days_within_3"] >= 1:
        return tiers[5]
    if counts["days_within_10"] >= 3:
        return tiers[6]
    if counts["days_within_10"] >= 1:
        return tiers[7]
    return tiers[8]


IMAGE_DIR = Path("record_images")
shutil.rmtree(IMAGE_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
IMAGE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
RUN_TOKEN = int(time.time())

DEBUG_RAISE = False  # False: a city that fails at any stage (bad station data,
                     # no usable candidate, etc.) is dropped with the reason
                     # logged, rather than taking down the whole page. Set
                     # True temporarily while chasing a specific failure.
failures = []


def run_stage(label, fn):
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        if DEBUG_RAISE:
            raise
        tb = traceback.format_exc().replace("--", "- -")
        failures.append((label, tb))
        return None


# Main map clip. Originally set to exactly 1 degree beyond four named
# reference cities (Edmonton north, San Francisco west, St. John's NL
# east, Puebla south), which correctly but literally cut off Oaxaca
# (~17.1°N, added in the same round as that clip rule) since it sits just
# south of that line. Revised here on request: south bound lowered to
# include Oaxaca with a bit of margin, and west bound pushed out well past
# San Francisco to open up more visible Pacific Ocean for the Alaska/
# Hawaii insets below (which were feeling cramped hugging the coastline).
# Oaxaca is still in CITIES and still fully resolved/tallied regardless of
# this line -- it only ever affects what's visible on this specific map.
MAIN_EXTENT = [-131.0, -51.7126, 16.0, 54.5461]

# Alaska (Anchorage, Fairbanks) and Hawaii (Honolulu) sit far outside
# MAIN_EXTENT -- rather than silently dropping them, both maps below give
# each its own small inset, positioned to sit within the Pacific Ocean
# portion of the main map itself (bottom-left, using the extra ocean space
# opened up by MAIN_EXTENT's western edge above) rather than as a
# separate panel outside the map's frame. Stacked directly on top of each
# other (Alaska above Hawaii) with a visible border around each, so they
# read as distinct panels rather than blending into the ocean entirely.
# Each shows the full state/island chain (not just a tight crop around its
# cities) -- Alaska's own extent stops at -180° rather than continuing
# across the antimeridian to the westernmost Aleutians, which would need
# real dateline-wraparound handling; this still captures the mainland,
# panhandle, and the large majority of the Aleutian chain by area and
# population. Both are labeled with the state/territory name at the top
# *and* each city with its own code, same as the main map. Alaska
# specifically uses its own Lambert Conformal projection (not the plain
# lon/lat grid PlateCarree uses) centered on Alaska -- PlateCarree
# visibly stretches high-latitude land east-west since it doesn't account
# for longitude lines converging toward the pole, which was making Alaska
# look wider than it really is; Cartopy's GeoAxes also never distorts a
# projection's true proportions to force-fit a panel's box shape (it
# letterboxes instead), so mismatched box vs. content aspect ratios show
# up as extra blank space around the map, not as a stretched result.
INSET_SPECS = [
    {
        "name": "Alaska", "rect": [0.015, 0.40, 0.20, 0.18],
        "extent": [-180, -130, 51, 72],
        "projection": ccrs.LambertConformal(central_longitude=-155, central_latitude=62),
    },
    {
        "name": "Hawaii", "rect": [0.015, 0.22, 0.20, 0.18],
        "extent": [-160.5, -154.5, 18.8, 22.5],
        "projection": ccrs.PlateCarree(),
    },
]


# Köppen-Geiger climate classification, for the reference map in section 9.
# Data: Beck, H.E., N.E. Zimmermann, T.R. McVicar, N. Vergopolan, A. Berg,
# E.F. Wood (2018): "Present and future Köppen-Geiger climate
# classification maps at 1-km resolution," Scientific Data 5:180214,
# https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2018.214 -- CC BY 4.0. Class codes and
# official RGB colors are exactly as published in that dataset's own
# legend.txt, not something invented for this page.
#
# The bundled file is a pre-cropped, pre-downsampled derivative, not the
# original download: the authors' own archive (fetched once, offline, to
# produce this file -- not at render time) ships the present-day
# classification at three resolutions, and koppen_na.npz here is their
# 5-arcmin ("0p083") grid cropped to North America (lon -180 to -50, lat
# 14 to 72) and gzip-compressed -- 45 KB, vs. the field's own coarsest
# full-globe file at roughly 10x that. Small enough to commit directly
# rather than fetching an external file at render time (this repo's own
# convention is normally the opposite -- see the README -- but a
# few-hundred-KB static classification grid is a different scale of
# problem than the multi-GB weather-model output other posts here
# legitimately fetch fresh each run).
KOPPEN_DATA_PATH = Path("data") / "koppen_na.npz"
KOPPEN_COLORS = {
    1: ("Af", "#0000FF"), 2: ("Am", "#0078FF"), 3: ("Aw", "#46AAFA"),
    4: ("BWh", "#FF0000"), 5: ("BWk", "#FF9696"), 6: ("BSh", "#F5A500"), 7: ("BSk", "#FFDC64"),
    8: ("Csa", "#FFFF00"), 9: ("Csb", "#C8C800"), 10: ("Csc", "#969600"),
    11: ("Cwa", "#96FF96"), 12: ("Cwb", "#64C864"), 13: ("Cwc", "#329632"),
    14: ("Cfa", "#C8FF50"), 15: ("Cfb", "#64FF50"), 16: ("Cfc", "#32C800"),
    17: ("Dsa", "#FF00FF"), 18: ("Dsb", "#C800C8"), 19: ("Dsc", "#963296"), 20: ("Dsd", "#966496"),
    21: ("Dwa", "#AAAFFF"), 22: ("Dwb", "#5A78DC"), 23: ("Dwc", "#4B50B4"), 24: ("Dwd", "#320087"),
    25: ("Dfa", "#00FFFF"), 26: ("Dfb", "#37C8FF"), 27: ("Dfc", "#007D7D"), 28: ("Dfd", "#00465F"),
    29: ("ET", "#B2B2B2"), 30: ("EF", "#666666"),
}
KOPPEN_GROUP_NAMES = {
    "A": "Tropical", "B": "Arid", "C": "Temperate", "D": "Continental (\"Cold\")", "E": "Polar",
}


def load_koppen_layer():
    """
    Returns (rgba_array, raw_class_codes, (left, right, bottom, top)).
    Class 0 (ocean / no classification, e.g. permanent ice sheets) is left
    fully transparent in rgba so the topography layer underneath shows
    through instead of a solid color standing in for "no data." The raw
    codes are returned too so callers (the legend below) don't need to
    re-open the file just to find out which classes are actually present.
    """
    npz = np.load(KOPPEN_DATA_PATH)
    codes = npz["data"]
    left, bottom, right, top = npz["bounds"]
    rgba = np.zeros((*codes.shape, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
    for code, (_, hex_color) in KOPPEN_COLORS.items():
        r, g, b = (int(hex_color[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5))
        rgba[codes == code] = (r, g, b, 255)
    return rgba, codes, (left, right, bottom, top)


def add_topography_underlay(axis, alpha=0.2):
    """
    A muted grayscale backdrop for the climate-zone map: Cartopy's own
    bundled Natural Earth shaded-relief raster (the same image
    ax.stock_img() uses), converted to grayscale and drawn at low opacity
    so it reads as subtle topographic texture rather than competing with
    the climate-zone colors on top of it. stock_img() itself doesn't
    expose grayscale conversion, hence loading the same file directly.
    """
    topo_path = (cartopy.config["repo_data_dir"] / "raster" / "natural_earth"
                 / "50-natural-earth-1-downsampled.png")
    topo_img = plt.imread(topo_path)
    gray = topo_img[..., :3].mean(axis=-1)
    axis.imshow(gray, cmap="gray", origin="upper", transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
                extent=[-180, 180, -90, 90], alpha=alpha, zorder=0)


def in_any_inset(df):
    mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
    for spec in INSET_SPECS:
        lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = spec["extent"]
        mask |= (df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)
    return mask


def in_main_extent(df):
    """
    A point outside set_extent() doesn't get a marker drawn (scatter
    respects the axes clip box), but annotate() draws its text regardless
    -- so without this filter, a city like Oaxaca that falls just outside
    MAIN_EXTENT (see the caveat where MAIN_EXTENT is defined) would show
    up as a code label floating below the map frame with no dot attached
    to it. Cities excluded here are still fully resolved and tallied
    elsewhere on the page; they just don't get plotted on this map.
    """
    lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = MAIN_EXTENT
    return (df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)


def add_basemap(axis):
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "land", "50m", edgecolor="none", facecolor="#f2f2f2"), zorder=0)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "physical", "coastline", "50m", edgecolor="#4d4d4d", facecolor="none"), linewidth=0.8, zorder=1)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "cultural", "admin_0_boundary_lines_land", "50m", edgecolor="#888888", facecolor="none"),
        linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
    axis.add_feature(cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature(
        "cultural", "admin_1_states_provinces_lakes", "50m", edgecolor="#bbbbbb", facecolor="none"),
        linewidth=0.4, zorder=1)


def plot_cities(axis, sub_df, show_labels=True, marker_color=None, s=70):
    """
    Scatter each city's point, optionally labeled with its short code
    (offset in fixed screen-space points, not data coordinates, so labels
    stay a legible fixed size regardless of the axes' zoom level).
    marker_color overrides each row's own "Tier color" with one fixed
    color for every point (used by the reference map in section 9, where
    every dot is plain black rather than tier-colored).
    """
    for _, row in sub_df.iterrows():
        axis.scatter(row["lon"], row["lat"], s=s, color=marker_color or row["Tier color"],
                     edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.5, transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(), zorder=5)
        if show_labels:
            axis.annotate(
                row["Code"], xy=(row["lon"], row["lat"]),
                xycoords=ccrs.PlateCarree()._as_mpl_transform(axis),
                xytext=(4, 3), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.5, zorder=6,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.7),
            )


def draw_insets(fig, df, basemap_fn=add_basemap, marker_color=None, s=70):
    """
    Shared by every map in this post that uses MAIN_EXTENT -- draws the
    Alaska/Hawaii insets defined in INSET_SPECS. basemap_fn lets the plain
    reference map (section 9) reuse this for its own stock_img() terrain
    background instead of the flat add_basemap() the tier-colored maps use,
    without duplicating the inset-layout logic itself.
    """
    for spec in INSET_SPECS:
        lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1 = spec["extent"]
        sub = df[(df["lon"] >= lon0) & (df["lon"] <= lon1) & (df["lat"] >= lat0) & (df["lat"] <= lat1)]
        inset_ax = fig.add_axes(spec["rect"], projection=spec["projection"])
        inset_ax.set_extent(spec["extent"], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())
        basemap_fn(inset_ax)
        if not sub.empty:
            plot_cities(inset_ax, sub, show_labels=True, marker_color=marker_color, s=s)
        inset_ax.text(0.5, 0.95, spec["name"], transform=inset_ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                       fontsize=7, fontweight="bold", zorder=10,
                       bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.75))
        for spine in inset_ax.spines.values():
            spine.set_visible(True)
            spine.set_edgecolor("#333333")
            spine.set_linewidth(1.0)


def render_temp_map(df, tiers, plot_title, output_path):
    """
    Shared by both the daily-high and daily-low maps below: draws the main
    map plus the Alaska/Hawaii insets, coloring each city's point by its
    assigned tier and labeling it with its short code. The legend is
    drawn on the figure itself as a horizontal band across the bottom
    (`fig.legend(..., loc="lower center")`), not off to the side, so the
    map above it can use almost the entire figure width.
    """
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 9))
    proj = ccrs.LambertConformal(central_longitude=-88, central_latitude=36)
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.005, 0.165, 0.99, 0.805], projection=proj)
    ax.set_extent(MAIN_EXTENT, crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())
    add_basemap(ax)
    plot_cities(ax, df[in_main_extent(df) & ~in_any_inset(df)])
    ax.set_title(plot_title, fontsize=13)

    draw_insets(fig, df)

    legend_handles = [
        plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", linestyle="none", markerfacecolor=color,
                   markeredgecolor="black", markersize=8, label=label)
        for color, label in tiers
    ]
    fig.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0),
               ncol=3, fontsize=8.5, framealpha=0.9)

    fig.savefig(output_path, format="png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)

2. Pull each station’s full daily high/low-temperature history
Fetched in parallel — each station’s history is an independent network call, and there’s no reason to wait for one before starting the next. Both the daily high and daily low come back in the same request per station, so adding the low-temperature analysis below didn’t require any extra fetching.

# Dev-only cache: while iterating on layout/rendering (not on the actual
# station-resolution logic), re-fetching ~250-500 station histories from
# Meteostat on every single test render was by far the slowest part of the
# feedback loop. With USE_LOCAL_CACHE = True, a station already fetched
# once this "session" is loaded from a local pickle instead of re-hit over
# the network -- CACHE_DIR is gitignored and never committed, so this
# changes nothing about what actually ships. MUST be False (the default)
# for the real render that gets pushed, since the cache doesn't know when
# a new month's data becomes available -- it would happily keep serving
# last month's fetch forever otherwise.
USE_LOCAL_CACHE = False
CACHE_DIR = Path("cache_dev")
if USE_LOCAL_CACHE:
    CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


def fetch_station_daily(station_id):
    cache_path = CACHE_DIR / f"{station_id}.pkl"
    if USE_LOCAL_CACHE and cache_path.exists():
        return pd.read_pickle(cache_path)
    ts = meteostat.daily(station_id, HIST_START, FETCH_END, parameters=[Parameter.TMAX, Parameter.TMIN])
    df = ts.fetch(units=UnitSystem.IMPERIAL)
    if USE_LOCAL_CACHE and df is not None:
        df.to_pickle(cache_path)
    return df


# Fetch every candidate for every city (not just the nearest one) so the
# best-populated station can be picked rather than just the closest one
# that clears a minimum bar. This matters: nearby() returns candidates by
# *distance*, and the physically closest site is sometimes a short-lived or
# sparsely-reporting station (e.g. a personal/community site) sitting right
# next to a much longer-running official airport station a few km further
# out. Picking "nearest that passes" over "most complete overall" was
# initially producing "records" built on a couple sparse decades instead of
# a station's full, well-populated history.
all_candidate_ids = sorted({sid for ids in city_candidates.values() for sid in ids})
station_data = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(fetch_station_daily, sid): sid for sid in all_candidate_ids}
    for future in futures:
        sid = futures[future]
        station_data[sid] = run_stage(f"station {sid} (fetch)", future.result)


MONTH_DATES = pd.date_range(TARGET_MONTH_START, TARGET_MONTH_END, freq="D")


def resolve_city(label, candidates):
    """
    Among this city's already-fetched candidate stations, pick whichever
    has the most actual years of daily-high history (not just whichever is
    nearest), is recent enough, and covers enough of the target month.
    Station choice is driven entirely by the high-temperature series --
    a station reporting both highs and lows normally has matching coverage
    for both, so this avoids running two separate (and possibly
    conflicting) candidate searches. Returns None (city dropped, reason
    logged) if no candidate qualifies.
    """
    reasons = []
    scored = []
    for station_id in candidates:
        df = station_data.get(station_id)
        if df is None or df.empty or "tmax" not in df.columns:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: no data returned")
            continue

        tmax_series = df["tmax"].dropna()
        if tmax_series.empty:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: no daily-high data returned")
            continue

        n_years = tmax_series.index.year.nunique()
        if n_years < MIN_RECORD_YEARS:
            reasons.append(f"{station_id}: only {n_years} year(s) of history")
            continue

        latest_available = tmax_series.index.max().date()
        if (TARGET_MONTH_END - latest_available).days > MAX_STALENESS_DAYS:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: most recent reading ({latest_available}) is more "
                f"than {MAX_STALENESS_DAYS} days before month-end {TARGET_MONTH_END}"
            )
            continue

        coverage = tmax_series.index.normalize().isin(MONTH_DATES).sum() / len(MONTH_DATES)
        if coverage < MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:
            reasons.append(
                f"{station_id}: only {coverage:.0%} of {TARGET_MONTH_START:%B %Y} covered "
                f"(need {MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE:.0%})"
            )
            continue

        tmin_series = df["tmin"].dropna() if "tmin" in df.columns else pd.Series(dtype=float)
        scored.append((n_years, station_id, tmax_series, tmin_series))

    if not scored:
        raise RuntimeError(f"No usable candidate station for {label}: " + "; ".join(reasons))

    # Most years of high-temp history wins, not nearest distance.
    n_years, station_id, tmax_series, tmin_series = max(scored, key=lambda t: t[0])
    return {
        "station": station_id, "n_years": n_years,
        "tmax_series": tmax_series, "tmin_series": tmin_series,
    }


results = {}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_WORKERS) as pool:
    futures = {
        pool.submit(resolve_city, label, city_candidates[label]): label
        for name, state, lat, lon, code in CITIES
        for label in [f"{name}, {state}"]
    }
    for future in futures:
        label = futures[future]
        result = run_stage(label, future.result)
        if result is not None:
            results[label] = result

print(f"Resolved {len(results)} / {len(CITIES)} cities for {TARGET_MONTH_START:%B %Y}.")

def expanding_daily_comparison(series, mode="max"):
    """
    For one station's full daily series (highs or lows), return a
    DataFrame (one row per date) with each day's reading compared against
    the expanding, backward-looking record for that calendar day -- i.e.
    the most extreme reading ever seen on that month/day in a *strictly
    earlier* year.

    mode="max" is for daily highs (record = highest prior reading);
    mode="min" is for daily lows (record = lowest prior reading, and the
    sign of diff_f is flipped so that diff_f > 0 always means "this day
    set a new record," regardless of mode -- callers never need to know
    which mode produced a given diff_f.

    Rows where fewer than MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES earlier years exist for that
    calendar day are dropped, not just rows with zero prior years. A
    station can pass the overall MIN_RECORD_YEARS bar and still have a
    calendar day's "record" resting on only a handful of early
    observations -- comparing against a record that immature makes it
    trivially easy to "beat," which would inflate every tally below with
    noise rather than genuine extremes.
    """
    df = series.rename("actual_f").to_frame()
    df["month"] = df.index.month
    df["day"] = df.index.day
    grouped = df.groupby(["month", "day"])["actual_f"]
    df["prior_n"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().count().shift(1))
    if mode == "max":
        df["prior_record_f"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().max().shift(1))
    else:
        df["prior_record_f"] = grouped.transform(lambda s: s.expanding().min().shift(1))
    df = df[df["prior_n"] >= MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES]
    if mode == "max":
        df["diff_f"] = (df["actual_f"] - df["prior_record_f"]).round(1)
    else:
        df["diff_f"] = (df["prior_record_f"] - df["actual_f"]).round(1)
    return df[["actual_f", "prior_record_f", "diff_f"]]

3. Back-calculated running tally since 2020 — daily highs
A single month is a small sample — most cities aren’t near their record in any given month. To get a real sense of how often major US cities are running hot relative to their own history, this section replays the comparison for every day since datetime.date(2020, 1, 1) through the end of the target month, for each of the 99 resolved cities (using the station histories already pulled above — no extra fetching needed), and keeps a cumulative tally across all of it. The per-day results computed here also feed directly into the monthly map in section 5.
The one thing that has to change for a multi-year replay: “the record” can’t be a fixed number looked up once, because it should only reflect what was actually the record at the time — a day in 2021 should be judged against the record as it stood coming into 2021, not against a hotter day that happened to occur in 2023. So for each station and each calendar day, this uses an expanding, backward-looking record: the highest reading ever seen on that calendar day in any earlier year. If a year sets a new record, that becomes the bar every later year is compared against — and, just as importantly, a year never gets compared against a record set after it.

section: Method notes & caveats
text:
Method notes & caveats

The city list is population plus judgment, not a single strict ranking. Population (~2023-2024 Census-era estimates) is the base proxy for “most influential” — there’s no single agreed-upon ranking for the latter, and population is the one that’s citable and doesn’t change based on opinion — but several rounds of manual additions/swaps followed: Dallas/Fort Worth/Arlington originally plotted three overlapping points in one metro area (trimmed to just Dallas); Oakland, Long Beach, Fresno, Mesa, and Baltimore were swapped for Billings MT, Boise ID, Sioux Falls SD, New Orleans LA, Salt Lake City UT, Birmingham AL, and St. Louis MO for broader geographic spread; a further 25 US cities (mostly state capitals and regionally notable cities named directly) were added, bringing the US total to 75; and Fairbanks AK and San Juan PR were added after that.
Canada and Mexico additions, “ignoring suburbs.” Both lists rank by city-proper population (not metro), which is what makes “ignoring suburbs” a real judgment call rather than a simple cutoff: a strict population ranking would include several satellite municipalities that are really just part of a bigger neighbor’s urban area — Mississauga, Brampton, and Surrey (Toronto/Vancouver suburbs in Canada); Ecatepec, Zapopan, and Guadalupe (Mexico City/Guadalajara/Monterrey suburbs in Mexico); and, on reflection, Tijuana’s inclusion was reconsidered and it was dropped too — all excluded even though several individually outrank cities that made the cut. The Canadian list went through several more passes after that: Hamilton, London, Kitchener, and Windsor were removed since, clustered together with Toronto and Ottawa, they made that corner of the map hard to read (even though none of the four is really a suburb in the Mississauga/Brampton sense); Victoria BC, Moncton NB, and St. John’s NL were added specifically to cover provinces that had zero representation otherwise; Gatineau QC was later removed too, once it became clear it was rendering as a second, effectively overlapping point right next to Ottawa at this map’s scale (its own distinct provincial government doesn’t help if the dot is indistinguishable from its neighbor’s); and Charlottetown PE — added for the same provincial- coverage reason as Victoria/Moncton/St. John’s, despite being notably smaller than everything else on the list — was itself later swapped for Kelowna BC. Ranking data for Mexican cities specifically is less precise here than for the US/Canada lists, so the exact cutoff toward the bottom of that list is approximate.
City codes. Every city gets a short, unique 2-3 character code, used to label its point on the maps in sections 5 and 8. Most are 3 characters, often that city’s real IATA airport code (ATL, PHX, MIA) — a recognizable 3-letter mnemonic beats a cryptic 2-letter one for most of these cities — though not always: Toronto’s real airport code is YYZ, but TOR reads far more clearly on a map, so a few codes favor clarity over the literal airport code. A handful of especially unambiguous cities (LA, SF, DC, KC, SJ) use 2 characters. The only hard requirement enforced is uniqueness across the whole list.
Data source: Meteostat, which aggregates NOAA/NWS (and other) station daily summaries. Station histories vary in length — some (e.g. long-running first-order airports) go back 80+ years; others considerably less. This is each station’s own digitized daily record, not necessarily an official NWS all-time record for that city (which may rely on a longer or differently-sourced period of record).
Why monthly, not daily: a single day is a noisy, low-signal snapshot, and daily reruns mostly re-fetched the same station histories for a one-day-later answer. Rendering once a month for the prior, fully completed month gives station data real time to finalize (some long-running stations lag by a week or more — see the staleness note below) and produces a more meaningful “how hot/cold did this month actually run” summary than a single day ever could.
Highs and lows share one mechanism, mirrored. expanding_daily_comparison() takes a mode argument (“max” for daily highs, “min” for daily lows) and internally flips the sign of diff_f for the “min” case, so that diff_f > 0 always means “this day set a new record in the extreme direction” regardless of which one is being computed. classify_diff() and classify_month() are likewise shared by both — only the color/label tables (MONTH_TIERS vs. MONTH_TIERS_MIN) and the category names (“Above record” vs. “Below record”) differ.
Station choice picks the most complete candidate, not the nearest one. Up to 5 candidates within 120 km are fetched for each city, and whichever has the most actual years of daily-high history is used — not whichever is physically closest. This was a deliberate fix after an initial version picked the nearest station unconditionally (as long as it cleared MIN_RECORD_YEARS), which for at least one test city turned out to be a nearby short/sparsely-reporting site instead of a much longer-running official airport station a few km further out. The same station (and thus the same daily-low series) is used for both the high-temperature and low-temperature analyses, rather than running two independent searches that could disagree.
A candidate station must also cover the target month. Beyond overall history length, MIN_MONTH_COVERAGE (80%) requires a candidate to have data for most of the target month specifically — a station can have decades of history and still have gone offline (or not yet reported) for the one month this page currently cares about.
Reporting lag / staleness: some stations’ daily summaries aren’t finalized for a couple of weeks. A candidate is rejected if its most recent reading is more than 21 days behind the target month’s end — generous on purpose, since the long-running official stations that make the best record sources also tend to have the slowest final QC lag.
A calendar day’s record also needs a minimum sample size of its own (MIN_PRIOR_SAMPLES = 15 earlier years). A station can pass the overall history-length bar while a specific month/day within it still has very few prior observations early in the record, making that day’s “record” trivially easy to beat — this floor keeps those thin spots out of every tally on this page.
The multi-year tallies and monthly maps use an expanding, backward-looking record. Comparing every day against the extreme over all years, including ones after it, would let e.g. a hot day in 2024 count as “the record” a 2020 reading is judged against, which reverses cause and effect. Instead, each day is compared only to the most extreme reading ever seen on that calendar day in a strictly earlier year, so a new record set in one year correctly moves the bar for every year after it, and never for years before it — see the worked spot-check in section 3, which finds a real (city, day) example and shows the record baseline actually changing over time rather than just asserting it does.
“Tied” means ±0.5°F, not ±1°F. An earlier version of this page used a ±1°F band (diff_f >= -1) for the “tied” tally category, which is a 2°F-wide window, not the 1°F-wide “within a degree” that was actually intended. TIED_BAND_F = 0.5 fixes this: “at record (tied)” now means -0.5 <= diff_f <= 0.5, a 1°F-wide band centered on the record.
“Sets a new record” means more than 0.5°F over, not more than 1°F. This threshold should pick up exactly where the tied band leaves off — it was briefly left at the old diff_f > 1 while TIED_BAND_F had already been tightened to 0.5, which left diff_f in (0.5, 1] classified as neither tied nor record-setting. classify_diff() now checks diff_f > TIED_BAND_F instead of a separately hardcoded 1, so the two bands share one boundary with nothing falling between them.
Why this color ladder (and why it’s not literally the first draft): it went through a few rounds. The very first version had two buckets defined identically (“< 3 days within 3°F” listed twice). The settled version is a 9-step diverging ladder: two fully-saturated anchor colors at the extremes, shading through progressively lighter tones toward a neutral gray in the middle, with each of the “tied” / “within 3°F” / “within 10°F” bands split into its own “3+ days” and “1-2 days” tier (checked 3+ first, so a city with 3+ days never gets miscounted into the “1-2” tier just because 1-2 is also technically true). One asymmetry worth calling out: the bottom tier’s label (“At least 1 day within 10°F”) is a holdover from before the “3+ days within 10°F” tier existed just above it — in practice that tier only ever fires for 1-2 days now, since 3+ is claimed first, but the exact wording wasn’t revisited.
Daily lows use the same ladder shape with the colors deliberately inverted. For daily highs, red means “notably hot” (close to or beyond the record) and blue means “far from the hot record, i.e. a relatively cool month.” For daily lows, blue instead means “notably cold” (close to or beyond the record low) and red means “far from the cold record, i.e. a relatively mild month” — matching the intuitive association of blue with cold and red with warm, at the cost of the two maps not sharing one universal color meaning (check each map’s own legend).
Why 2020 for the multi-year tally: 2020 was chosen as a round, recent starting point with enough span to show a year-over-year pattern rather than just one data point; there’s nothing special about that year beyond that.
DEBUG_RAISE = False: a city that fails at any stage (no usable station, insufficient history, stale data, insufficient month coverage, or — for the low-temperature analysis specifically — a station that reports highs but not lows) is dropped, with the reason logged as an HTML comment in the page source, rather than taking down the whole page. Flip it to True temporarily to get a full traceback while debugging a specific city.
Meteostat’s own per-station-year load failures are logged, not printed to the page. A transient network hiccup fetching one year out of a station’s multi-decade history is something Meteostat already handles gracefully on its own (that year is just dropped; the rest of the fetch continues) – but by default it does so via a stdlib logging.warning(..., exc_info=True) call that, with no handler configured anywhere in this notebook, printed a full traceback straight into the rendered page’s output. logging.getLogger("meteostat").setLevel(logging.ERROR) in the setup cell raises Meteostat’s own log threshold so that noise doesn’t surface, without touching this page’s own failure reporting (run_stage/failures) below.
Large-request guard disabled on purpose: Meteostat blocks any single daily-data request spanning more than 30 years by default. That’s turned off here (meteostat.config.block_large_requests = False) deliberately, since computing an honest “record for this calendar day” requires each station’s entire digitized history, not just the last 30 years.
Station fetches run in parallel (ThreadPoolExecutor, up to 16 at once) since each is an independent network call to Meteostat’s bulk data. Every candidate for every city is fetched (not just the nearest one, per the station-choice note above), so this stage pulls roughly 5x more station histories than there are cities — still well worth parallelizing, but it’s the long pole in this page’s render time. N_WORKERS was raised from 10 to 16 when the city list doubled from 50 to 100, to keep the total render from simply doubling too; expect somewhere in the 20-30 minute range for all 100 cities. That’s a real cost, but at a monthly cadence it’s a non-issue.
Canada and Mexico station coverage is untested territory. Meteostat aggregates station data globally, not just US NOAA/NWS sources, so the same resolve_city logic (longest history, target-month coverage, staleness) is applied to Canadian and Mexican candidates with no special casing. Whether those regions have as many long-running, densely-covered stations within STATION_SEARCH_RADIUS_M as US cities typically do is genuinely unknown until a render actually runs — if a Canadian or Mexican city is missing from a given month’s map, check the HTML source comments for why (same DEBUG_RAISE/failures mechanism as any other city).
The main map is deliberately clipped, not a loose “fit everything” extent. MAIN_EXTENT is defined as exactly 1° beyond four named reference points — north of Edmonton, west of San Francisco, east of St. John’s NL, south of Puebla (“Pueblo” as given was read as Puebla, the only spelling used anywhere else in this file; a literal Pueblo, CO reading would cut off all of Mexico, which can’t be right given Mexican cities were being added in the same request). One real consequence: with Puebla itself removed from CITIES in this same round, Oaxaca (added at the same time, ~17.1°N) now sits just south of that clip line and won’t actually show up on the main map, even though it’s still in the city list and still fully tallied — a direct side effect of taking the clip instruction literally rather than quietly padding it out to fit every city that happened to get added alongside it.
Alaska and Hawaii get their own insets, positioned inside the map’s own Pacific Ocean space rather than as a separate outside panel — bottom-left, roughly where the ocean west of Mexico/California actually is on this projection. Both are zoomed in tight (Oahu only for Hawaii; the Anchorage/Fairbanks corridor for Alaska) and labeled with just the state name at the top rather than per-city codes, since there isn’t room for a recognizable shape and readable per-city labels at this size. Insets are defined purely by their own geographic extent (a lon/lat box), not a hardcoded city list, so both Alaska cities land in the same inset automatically. Alaska specifically uses its own Lambert Conformal projection centered on Alaska rather than the plain PlateCarree grid — PlateCarree visibly stretches high-latitude land east-west (it doesn’t account for longitude lines converging toward the pole), which was making Alaska look wider than it actually is.
The legend is back inside the map image, as a horizontal band across the bottom. An earlier version moved it to a separate HTML color-key below the image instead, to stop it from competing with the map for space — reversed here in favor of a single self-contained image, now laid out as fig.legend(..., loc="lower center", ncol=3) instead of the tall single-column list on the right that a plain matplotlib legend defaults to, so it still doesn’t eat much vertical room. City-code labels are also 1pt larger than the first version of this layout (6.5pt, up from 5.5pt) now that there’s more room to work with.
The bottom tier’s label now matches what the code actually checks. It previously read “Not close all month (<3 days within 20°F),” but classify_month() never actually checks a 20°F band anywhere — that tier is reached purely as the fallback once every narrower band above it (down to “at least 1 day within 10°F”) has failed to match, i.e. zero days came within 10°F all month. Relabeled to “No days within 10°F of record” (or “…of record low”) to say exactly that instead of describing a threshold the code doesn’t use.
Dense clusters of cities can produce overlapping code labels. Labels are placed with a small fixed pixel offset from each point, not by any collision-avoidance algorithm — in a tightly-packed region (e.g. the Boston-New York-Philadelphia-DC corridor, or the Toronto/Ottawa area), some labels may overlap or sit close enough to be hard to read at a glance. The underlying monthly_df / monthly_df_min tables above each map list every city’s code unambiguously if a label on the map itself is unclear.
Section 9’s climate-zone layer is real Köppen-Geiger classification data, not a terrain-shading stand-in. An earlier version of this page used Cartopy’s bundled Natural Earth shaded-relief raster (ax.stock_img()) as a rough visual proxy and was explicit that it was not a genuine climate classification. That’s since been replaced with the actual thing: Beck, H.E., N.E. Zimmermann, T.R. McVicar, N. Vergopolan, A. Berg, E.F. Wood (2018), “Present and future Köppen-Geiger climate classification maps at 1-km resolution,” Scientific Data 5:180214, doi:10.1038/sdata.2018.214, CC BY 4.0 — the standard modern reference for this classification, and the same one most published Köppen maps (including the one linked when this feature was requested) are ultimately built from. Class codes and colors are exactly as published in the dataset’s own legend.txt, not invented for this page. The Natural Earth shaded-relief raster is still present, but demoted to a muted, low-opacity (20%) grayscale backdrop underneath the climate colors (add_topography_underlay()), rather than the main layer — geographic/topographic context, not the focus.
The Köppen data is bundled with the repo, not fetched at render time — a deliberate exception to this site’s usual practice (see the README, and how every other live-data post here fetches fresh each run). The published dataset ships the present-day classification at three resolutions; koppen_na.npz here is the 5-arcmin (“0p083”) grid, cropped once (offline, not at render time) to lon -180 to -50 / lat 14 to 72 and gzip-compressed to 45 KB. That’s a different scale of problem than the multi-GB weather-model output other posts on this site legitimately fetch fresh each run, and unlike a live external fetch, it can’t fail or change format out from under a future scheduled render — worth it here since the classification itself doesn’t change month-to-month the way weather does.
Alaska and Hawaii’s insets show the (approximately) full state/territory, not just a tight crop around their cities. Alaska’s own extent stops at -180° rather than continuing across the antimeridian to the westernmost Aleutian islands, which would need real dateline-wraparound handling to render correctly — this still captures the mainland, panhandle, and the large majority of the Aleutian chain by both area and population. Cartopy’s GeoAxes never distorts a projection’s true proportions to force-fit a panel’s box shape (it letterboxes — adds blank space — instead), so a mismatch between an inset’s box aspect ratio and its content’s true aspect ratio shows up as extra margin around the map, not as visible stretching.

Keeping this page current
Unlike the tropical cyclone outlook post (which needs to refresh daily while a storm is active), this page only needs to refresh once a month, since it’s summarizing a full completed month at a time. It’s rendered on its own monthly schedule — see .github/workflows/publish.yml for the actual cron job — separate from the site’s daily/push-triggered rebuild, so it isn’t re-fetching ~250 station histories (a 15-20 minute job) on every push to this repo.

title: NHC Tropical Cyclone Outlook: Rainfall & Max Sustained Wind within 500 km
text:
Every time this page is rendered (including the scheduled daily rebuild — see the note at the bottom), it:

Pulls every currently active NHC storm across the Atlantic, East Pacific, and Central Pacific basins.
For each one, downloads its official forecast track and classifies each point by Saffir-Simpson category.
Pulls matching HAFS (Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System) fields – accumulated precipitation and a period-maximum surface wind – masks each field to a 500 km circle around the storm’s forecast position at each step, sums rainfall across steps, and takes the running maximum wind seen at each pixel across the entire forecast period.
Renders one plot per storm (as a real PNG file, not an embedded image — see the caveats), and gives you a dropdown to switch between them.

The steps below are broken into the same stages, each ending with a small table or plot summarizing what that stage produced – useful both for following along and for spotting a bad storm before it reaches the final map.






Important



This dropdown does not recompute anything live. The site is static — there’s no server behind it. At render time, this code pre-computes a plot for every active storm; the dropdown just shows/hides a pre-rendered image. What you see is only as fresh as the last render (daily, via cron).




Code
import re
import shutil
import time
import traceback
import zipfile
import io
import os
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

# Force PROJ (used by pyproj/cartopy/fiona) to read its database from the
# conda env actually running this notebook (sys.prefix), not whatever
# PROJ_DATA/PROJ_LIB the parent shell happens to have exported -- e.g. an
# older PROJ install from a different conda env on the same machine. A
# mismatched, older proj.db raises "DATABASE.LAYOUT.VERSION.MINOR ... whereas
# a number >= 6 is expected." Must run before geopandas/pyproj/cartopy import.
os.environ["PROJ_DATA"] = os.path.join(sys.prefix, "share", "proj")
os.environ.pop("PROJ_LIB", None)

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests
import xarray as xr
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from pyproj import Geod
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy.feature as cfeature

# --- Configuration -----------------------------------------------------
RADIUS_KM = 500.0
BASINS = {"al": "NA", "ep": "EP", "cp": "CP"}  # NHC's own Atlantic prefix is "al"
# EXTENT_PAD_DEG is the final map's zoom level; BBOX_PAD_DEG is how far past
# that the underlying HAFS regridding domain extends, so the fetched data
# always covers a margin beyond what's actually shown (avoids a blank strip
# right at the visible edge). Keep BBOX_PAD_DEG > EXTENT_PAD_DEG by the same
# margin if you change either.
BBOX_PAD_DEG = 15.0
EXTENT_PAD_DEG = 10.0
CURRENT_STORMS_URL = "https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/CurrentStorms.json"
HAFS_MODEL = "hafsa"
HAFS_PRODUCT = "storm.atm"
HAFS_MAX_FXX = 126
GEOD = Geod(ellps="WGS84")

MM_TO_IN = 1.0 / 25.4
MPS_TO_MPH = 2.236936
ONE_MIN_SUSTAINED_FACTOR = 1.0 / 0.88  # WMO 10-min -> 1-min rule-of-thumb; not an official NHC value

# Precip colorbar: log scale so the 1-10 in range (where most of the
# interesting variation is) isn't washed out by rare, very high values.
# Capped at 30 in -- anything above renders as the top color (colorbar shows
# a ">" arrow via extend="max") rather than stretching the whole scale to
# accommodate one extreme pixel.
PRECIP_VMIN_IN = 1.0
PRECIP_VMAX_IN = 30.0

# Images are written as real PNG files (NOT embedded base64 -- Quarto's
# preview server tried to treat a base64 data: URI as a filesystem path and
# crashed with "File name too long"). RUN_TOKEN is appended as a query
# string on every <img> src so your browser can't serve a stale cached copy
# of a file that has the same name across renders.
IMAGE_DIR = Path("storm_images")
shutil.rmtree(IMAGE_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
IMAGE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
RUN_TOKEN = int(time.time())

# Intensity-ordered warm ramp (amber -> orange -> red -> pink), least to
# most intense -- not NHC's own official category colors.
CATEGORY_COLORS = {"TD": "#FDA429", "TS": "#FB6107", "HU": "#E4003A", "MH": "#C3008F", "Unknown": "#999999"}
CATEGORY_LABELS = {
    "TD": "Tropical Depression", "TS": "Tropical Storm",
    "HU": "Hurricane (Cat 1-2)", "MH": "Major Hurricane (Cat 3+)", "Unknown": "Unknown",
}
WIND_CONTOUR_COLOR = "black"
WIND_SMOOTH_SIGMA = 3  # gaussian smoothing bandwidth, in grid cells
LAND_FILL_COLOR = "#e2e2e2"
LAND_BORDER_COLOR = "#4d4d4d"

DEBUG_RAISE = False  # False: a storm that fails at any stage below (e.g. no
                     # HAFS data yet for a brand-new invest) is skipped for
                     # the remaining stages -- reason logged as an HTML
                     # comment -- rather than taking down the whole page.
                     # Set True temporarily while chasing a specific failure
                     # to get Quarto's own full-traceback error reporting.
failures = []  # (label, traceback) pairs accumulated across every stage


def run_stage(label, fn):
    """
    Run a zero-argument callable for one storm at one pipeline stage,
    honoring DEBUG_RAISE. Returns fn()'s result, or None if this storm
    failed at this stage (and should be dropped from later stages).
    """
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        if DEBUG_RAISE:
            raise
        tb = traceback.format_exc().replace("--", "- -")
        failures.append((label, tb))
        return None


def classify_category(wind_kt):
    if wind_kt is None or (isinstance(wind_kt, float) and np.isnan(wind_kt)):
        return "Unknown"
    if wind_kt < 34:
        return "TD"
    if wind_kt < 64:
        return "TS"
    if wind_kt < 96:
        return "HU"
    return "MH"


def geodesic_circle(center_lon, center_lat, radius_km, n=72):
    az = np.linspace(0, 360, n, endpoint=True)
    lon2, lat2, _ = GEOD.fwd(np.full(n, center_lon), np.full(n, center_lat),
                              az, np.full(n, radius_km * 1000.0))
    return lon2, lat2


def circle_mask_km(lon2d, lat2d, center_lon, center_lat, radius_km):
    n = lon2d.size
    grid_lons = np.where(lon2d.ravel() > 180, lon2d.ravel() - 360, lon2d.ravel())
    _, _, dist_m = GEOD.inv(np.full(n, center_lon), np.full(n, center_lat), grid_lons, lat2d.ravel())
    return (dist_m / 1000.0 <= radius_km).reshape(lon2d.shape)


def smooth_for_contour(da, sigma=WIND_SMOOTH_SIGMA):
    """
    Gaussian-smooth a 2D field for prettier contour lines, without letting
    NaN (outside the 500 km composite footprint) bleed a false gradient into
    the valid region. Standard "fill with 0, smooth the validity mask the
    same way, divide back out" trick, then re-mask anywhere the smoothed
    validity weight is too low to trust.
    """
    values = da.values
    valid = np.isfinite(values)
    if not valid.any():
        return da
    filled = np.where(valid, values, 0.0)
    smoothed = gaussian_filter(filled, sigma=sigma)
    weight = gaussian_filter(valid.astype(float), sigma=sigma)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        result = smoothed / weight
    result[weight < 0.2] = np.nan
    return da.copy(data=result)


def atcf_storm_id(nhc_id):
    nhc_id = nhc_id.lower()
    basin_letter = {"al": "l", "ep": "e", "cp": "c"}[nhc_id[:2]]
    return f"{nhc_id[2:4]}{basin_letter}"


def first_data_var(ds):
    skip = {"latitude", "longitude", "time", "step", "valid_time",
            "surface", "isobaricInhPa", "heightAboveGround"}
    for name in ds.data_vars:
        if name not in skip:
            return ds[name]
    raise RuntimeError(f"No data variable found in dataset: {list(ds.data_vars)}")


def best_matching_bucket(H, var_search, end_hour):
    """Widest available bucket for var_search that ends exactly at end_hour."""
    try:
        inv = H.inventory(var_search)
    except Exception:
        return None
    if inv is None or len(inv) == 0:
        return None
    pattern = re.compile(r"(\d+)-(\d+) hour")
    best, best_width = None, -1
    for _, row in inv.iterrows():
        m = pattern.search(str(row.get("forecast_time", "")))
        if not m:
            continue
        start, end = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))
        if end == end_hour and (end - start) > best_width:
            best, best_width = row["search_this"], end - start
    return best
